report.tagline: Atlassian's Jira is the tool most software teams use to plan, track and ship work, sold alongside Confluence, Loom and the Rovo AI.
report.simpleSummary: Jira is a to-do board for teams, built first for software engineers. Each piece of work is a ticket that moves across a board from 'To do' to 'Done', so everyone can see who is doing what. Atlassian, an Australian company, also makes Confluence for documents and Loom for video. It famously grew without a big sales team: teams found it online, tried it free and paid by card.

overview.whatItDoes: Jira lets teams plan and track work as tickets on boards, backlogs and timelines. Software teams use it for sprints and bugs; business and service teams use Jira Service Management for help desks. Atlassian sells it with Confluence (wiki), Loom (video), Bitbucket (code) and Rovo, an AI that searches and acts across all of a company's tools.
howItWorks: A team signs up for Jira Cloud free for up to 10 users.
They create a project and add tickets (issues) for each task or bug.
Tickets move through a workflow on a Scrum or Kanban board.
Jira connects to GitHub, Slack, Figma and over 3,000 Marketplace apps.
As the team grows, it pays per user per month on Standard or Premium plans.
Large companies buy Enterprise plans, and are being moved off self-hosted Data Center to Cloud.
overview.valueProposition: One place where everyone can see what work exists, who owns it and where it stands, flexible enough for any team's process.

businessModel.summary: Atlassian makes money from per-user subscriptions for Jira, Confluence and its other tools, mostly in the cloud. Most small customers buy online without talking to sales, which keeps the cost of getting a customer low. Big companies pay much more for Enterprise plans.

revenueStreams.detail: Per user per month for Jira, Confluence, Loom and more. $4.41 billion in FY26.
Self-hosted versions for large companies, $1.83 billion in FY26, being phased out by 2029.
Atlassian takes a cut of partner apps sold on its Marketplace.
Higher tiers with more admin, security and Rovo AI features.

businessModel.pricing: Jira Free for up to 10 users. Standard about $7.50 per user per month and Premium about $13.50 per user per month (2025 to 2026 list prices, lower per user at large seat counts). Enterprise custom.
costDrivers: Research and development, the largest cost
businessModel.unitEconomics: A 50-person team on Jira Standard pays about 50 x $7.50 = $375 a month, or $4,500 a year. Hosting costs are a small share, so gross margin is over 80%. Because most small teams buy online, the cost to win them is low. Over time they add Confluence and move to Premium, so spend per customer grows. That is why Atlassian earns $1.3 billion in free cash flow even with a small GAAP loss. Rough estimates.

howTheyGetUsers: Product-led growth: teams find, try and buy without sales
Free plan for up to 10 users
Engineers bringing Jira from job to job
Cross-selling Confluence, Loom and Jira Service Management to existing customers
whatBringsUsersBack: Daily standups and sprints run on Jira boards
Tickets are where tasks get assigned
Integrations push updates from code and chat
Years of project history stored in Jira
growth.moat: Big companies build custom workflows, reports and Marketplace apps on Jira over years, so moving away is slow and risky. Atlassian also argues its 'Teamwork Graph', the map of who works on what, gives its AI context that rivals cannot hire or copy.

competitors.name: Linear
competitors.positioning: Fast, simple issue tracker loved by startups.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Linear is faster and cleaner. Jira is more flexible and fits large, complex companies.

competitors.name: Monday.com, Asana, ClickUp
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: They are easier for non-engineers. Jira is deeper for software teams.

competitors.name: GitHub Issues and Projects
competitors.positioning: Tracking built into where code lives.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: GitHub is simpler and closer to code. Jira has richer planning and reports.

competitors.name: ServiceNow
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Jira Service Management is cheaper and faster to set up.

guardrailMetrics: Customers lost during Data Center to Cloud migration
strengths: Default tool for software teams, used by over 85% of the Fortune 500
Strong cash flow of $1.3 billion a year
weaknesses: Seen as slow, complex and cluttered
Engineers often dislike it, even when managers pick it
Forced Data Center end-of-life upsets some large customers
Growth will slow to about 13% in FY27
risks: Linear and GitHub winning new startups
AI coding agents changing how software work is planned
Customers leaving during the forced Cloud migration
Big spending on AI and deals like The Browser Company with unclear returns
userComplaints: 2025 navigation changes made the experience worse, according to admin forums
Too many fields and steps to create a ticket
Data Center price hikes and end-of-life push

improvementIdeas.idea: A 'fast mode' for engineers: keyboard-first, minimal fields, instant load
improvementIdeas.problem: Engineers find Jira slow and cluttered and prefer Linear.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: Better engineer satisfaction, fewer startups switching to Linear.
improvementIdeas.metricToTrack: Board load time and tickets completed per engineer

improvementIdeas.idea: Rovo writes and updates tickets from Slack threads and pull requests
improvementIdeas.metricToTrack: Share of tickets created or updated by Rovo

improvementIdeas.idea: Migration guarantee: free help and price lock for Data Center customers
improvementIdeas.problem: Large customers are upset by the forced move.
improvementIdeas.metricToTrack: Data Center to Cloud migration completion rate

improvementIdeas.idea: One-click leadership summary of all projects
improvementIdeas.problem: PMs spend hours on status reports.
improvementIdeas.expectedImpact: Saves time and raises Premium upgrades.

pmLessons: Product-led growth lets a company reach hundreds of thousands of customers without a big sales team, if users can try and buy alone.
Flexibility wins big customers but creates complexity that annoys everyday users.
Moving customers to a new model, like Cloud, raises long-term revenue but risks losing them during the switch.
The person who buys a tool is often not the person who uses it, so you must design for both.

interviewQuestions.question: Engineers hate Jira but companies keep buying it. Why, and what would you do?
interviewQuestions.hint: Separate buyer (managers, admins) from user (engineers). Explain value for each. Propose a fix for users that keeps buyer value.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you stop startups from choosing Linear?
interviewQuestions.hint: Find why they pick Linear (speed, simplicity). Propose a lighter Jira, better onboarding. Track new team sign-ups.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you measure Rovo's success?
interviewQuestions.hint: Weekly active users, tasks completed by agents, time saved, effect on renewal.

interviewQuestions.question: Atlassian grew without a big sales team. How does that work?
interviewQuestions.hint: Free plan, self-serve buying, word of mouth, expansion inside accounts, low cost to win customers.

interviewQuestions.question: What is Jira's north star metric?
interviewQuestions.hint: Teams completing work weekly. Break into new teams, tickets done, expansion, AI use.
